passage: I sat behind Tushar in the cafeteria when two boys from our own hostel block spilt trays and shouted at the staff. Tushar shrugged and said, "They just had a bad day." A week later two boys from the other block did the same thing, and Tushar said loudly, "Typical. Those people always behave like this." Ojas, at our table, raised an eyebrow. "You said bad day last week," said Ojas. Tushar blinked. "That was different." I could tell Tushar believed it. I do not think Tushar has noticed the double standard yet.

qa.q: What did Tushar say when two boys from Tushar's own hostel block spilt trays?
qa.a: Tushar said, "They just had a bad day."

qa.q: What does Tushar's "That was different" suggest about what Tushar believes?
qa.a: It suggests Tushar honestly believes the two cases differ and has not noticed the double standard; the blink shows surprise rather than deceit.

qa.q: What could Ojas do next time to help Tushar see it without an argument?
qa.a: Ojas could ask a gentle question, such as "What was different?", and let Tushar answer, instead of only pointing out the contradiction.

qa.q: How might Ojas be feeling when raising an eyebrow and repeating "You said bad day last week"?
qa.a: Ojas is probably a little puzzled or irritated by the unfairness, and speaks up while keeping the tone light enough to leave Tushar room to think.

grounding: A young adult sees a bad act by their own group as an individual mistake but a similar act by another group as typical, a double standard that feels natural.

passage: Monday. After the derby, three fans in Simran's club scarf threw bottles at the away stand. "A few idiots," Simran told Manjula. Wednesday. Photos showed three fans of the other club doing the same. "See? That whole club is savages," said Simran, scrolling. Manjula put down her phone. "Last week it was a few idiots." Saturday. Simran walked past the stand and saw both sets of fans clearing bottles together after a charity match. Simran remembered the words "a few idiots" and said to Manjula, "I said two different things about the same act." Manjula nodded.

qa.q: What did Simran say about the three fans in Simran's club scarf?
qa.a: Simran said they were "a few idiots".

qa.q: What was Simran feeling on Saturday when remembering "a few idiots"?
qa.a: Simran felt a jolt of realisation and some embarrassment at having judged the same act by two different standards.

qa.q: What turning point helped Simran notice the double standard?
qa.a: Manjula quietly repeated "Last week it was a few idiots", and later the sight of both sets of fans clearing bottles together made the contradiction plain.

qa.q: What might Manjula have been feeling when putting down her phone and repeating Simran's earlier words?
qa.a: Manjula was probably uneasy at the unfairness and chose a calm reminder rather than an accusation, leaving Simran room to notice.

grounding: A young adult sees a bad act by their own group as an individual mistake but a similar act by another group as typical, a double standard that goes unnoticed.

passage:
At the college hostel meeting, the warden read out the damages: two broken chairs in the girls' common room, one torn curtain.
“That was just Priyanka being silly with a birthday cake fight,” Lakshmi told the girls near her. “She's not like that normally.”
Everyone nodded.
Last month, when the boys' hostel broke a table, Lakshmi had said, “Typical boys' hostel. They're all animals.”
Mohit, from the student council, was sitting in the row behind. He leaned forward. “So when it's your side it's one person, and when it's ours it's everyone?”
Lakshmi laughed. “That's different.” She couldn't say how. She turned back to the warden, a little annoyed, and forgot about it by dinner.

qa.q: What did the warden read out as damaged?
qa.a: Two broken chairs in the girls' common room and one torn curtain.

qa.q: How did Lakshmi feel when Mohit pointed out the difference?
qa.a: She felt annoyed and a little defensive, laughing it off without being able to explain why it was different.

qa.q: What could Lakshmi try to check her own fairness?
qa.a: She could ask herself whether she'd say the same thing if the other hostel had done it, before judging.

qa.q: How might Mohit see Lakshmi's comments?
qa.a: He likely finds them unfair and a bit frustrating, since his hostel is judged as a whole while hers gets excused.

grounding: Shows a young woman excusing her own hostel's damage as one person's mistake while calling a similar act by another group typical.

passage:
Dear Anjali,
The inter-college quiz was a mess! You'll hear stories, so here's the truth.
One of our team, Nikhil, was caught reading answers off his phone in the second round. Honestly, that's just Nikhil. One silly guy under pressure. Our college is not like that at all.
But the other team, from Riverside College, had a guy who kept looking at his friend's paper. That's so typical of Riverside. Everyone knows their students cheat. It's the culture there.
Anyway, we got disqualified, which was unfair. The judges should have looked at Riverside too.
Come for the fest next month. We'll show you how it's done.
Bhupen

qa.q: Which round was Nikhil caught in?
qa.a: He was caught in the second round.

qa.q: How does Bhupen seem to feel about the disqualification?
qa.a: Bhupen feels it was unfair and is annoyed, defensive about his own college while blaming Riverside.

qa.q: What would you advise Bhupen to notice in his own letter?
qa.a: Bhupen could notice that the letter calls Nikhil's cheating one person's mistake but Riverside's as "typical", and judge both the same way.

qa.q: How might a Riverside student feel reading this letter?
qa.a: They would likely feel insulted and unfairly lumped together because of one student's behaviour.

grounding: A young adult writes a letter excusing the home college's cheater as one person but calling another college's cheating typical.

passage:
So you want to hear about our trekking club? I'm Harsha, and I'll tell you about the time Uma caught me out.
We were on a trek near Coorg. One of our guys, Sameer, threw a chips packet into the valley. I said, “Arre, Sameer, pick it up,” and laughed. He's just careless sometimes.
The next day, we saw a group of tourists from another city leave bottles at a viewpoint. I said loudly, “Typical city people. No respect for nature.”
Uma, our club leader, stopped walking. “Harsha, yesterday Sameer did the same thing. Is he typical of us?”
I had no answer. I actually hadn't noticed. It felt so natural to think our guy was just one guy, and they were all the same.

qa.q: Where was the trek?
qa.a: The trek was near Coorg.

qa.q: How did Harsha feel when Uma pointed out the double standard?
qa.a: Harsha felt caught out and embarrassed, having no answer and not having noticed it before.

qa.q: What could Harsha do differently on the next trek?
qa.a: Harsha could treat every littering the same way, asking anyone to pick it up, whoever they are.

qa.q: How might Uma have felt watching both moments?
qa.a: Uma probably felt frustrated by the unfairness, which is why Uma stopped walking to point it out.

grounding: A young adult recalls excusing a friend's littering as one person's slip while calling strangers' littering typical of their group.

passage:
Tuesday: In the hostel common room, Rekha found the kettle crusted and cups piled in the sink. "Classic C-wing," she told Mohit and Anu. "That whole wing is careless."
Friday: The kettle was crusted again. This time Anu had seen who did it: Priya, from Rekha's own A-wing. "Oh, Priya's had three exams this week," Rekha said. "She's just stressed. It's a one-off."
Sunday: Mohit, washing cups, said lightly, "So when C-wing does it, it's the wing, and when Priya does it, it's the exams?"
Rekha laughed. "That's different. You don't know Priya." She went back to her phone and didn't notice Mohit and Anu exchange a look.

qa.q: Who from A-wing left the kettle crusted on Friday?
qa.a: Priya, from Rekha's own A-wing.

qa.q: Why did Rekha excuse Priya so easily?
qa.a: Rekha felt protective and loyal toward someone from her own wing, so Priya's mess seemed like a stressed one-off.

qa.q: What question could Rekha ask herself before blaming a whole group next time?
qa.a: Whether she would say the same about her own wing if one of them did it, or whether she even knows who did it.

qa.q: How might the C-wing students feel if they heard Rekha on Tuesday?
qa.a: They would likely feel unfairly judged and annoyed, blamed as a whole wing for what one unknown person did.

grounding: Shows a young adult excusing a mess by her own wing as a one-off while blaming another wing's similar mess on the whole group, without noticing.
